en: *Śivasvarodaya* (Kaivalyadhama edition, 2015), transcribed by Lubomír Ondračka:
*śrī gaṇeśāya namaḥ* Having paid homage to Maheśvara, to the Daughter of the Mountain, and to the Leader of the Gaṇas, [the author speaks].
I worship the Guru, the Supreme Self, the deliverer from the cycle of worldly existence.
(1) The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, having bestowed your grace upon me—
O Lord, tell me the knowledge that brings about all accomplishments.
How was the cosmic egg produced, and how does it revolve?
O God, tell me the definitive account of how the cosmic egg dissolves.
Īśvara said:
From the *tattva* the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is produced; by the *tattva* it revolves;
into the *tattva* it dissolves, O Goddess. Thus is the determination of the cosmic egg from the *tattva*. (4)
The Goddess said:
"The ultimate reality alone is determined by the proponents of truth to be the supreme root.
O Lord, what is the nature of that reality? Please reveal that very reality."
The Lord said: Maheśvara is the one God, stainless and formless;
from him the ether was produced, and from the ether the wind arose.
From wind arose fire, from that water, and from that the earth was produced;
these five elements expanded in fivefold ways. From them the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) was born, and by them alone it is sustained.
It dissolves right there and again delights right there.
O beautiful one, within the body composed of the five elements, the five elements exist in a subtle form; they are known by those yogis who perceive reality.
Now I shall explain the *svara* [science], the arising of sound from the body; through the nature of the movement of the *haṃsa*, knowledge born of the three times arises.
This essence, more secret than the secret, is a revelation of assistance.
This knowledge of the rising of breath (Svarodaya) is a jewel upon the crest of all forms of knowledge.
It is a wisdom subtler than the subtle, easily understood, and based on truth;
it is a marvel in the world of the atheist, yet a firm support for the person of faith.

Now, regarding the characteristics of a disciple: the Svarodaya should be imparted only to one who is tranquil, pure, of virtuous conduct, whose mind is solely devoted to the guru, firm of heart, and grateful. (13)

Knowledge of the voice is not given to one who is wicked, malicious, angry, an atheist, a violator of the guru’s bed, lacking in strength, or of evil conduct. Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme knowledge situated within the body as it is being told.
By means of which mere consciousness omniscience is attained.
||15|| In sound are the Vedas and the Shastras; in sound is the supreme Gandharva art; in sound is the entire triple world; sound is the very nature of the Self. ||16||
An astrologer devoid of the musical notes (svara) is like a house without a master, like a face without a scripture, or like a body without a head;
likewise [useless] is one who does not know the divisions of the channels (nāḍī), the vital breath (prāṇa), and the divisions of the principles (tattva). ||17||

He who knows the distinction between the Suṣumnā and the mixed [channels] attains liberation. Whether in the formed or the formless state, some say that auspiciousness is produced by the power of the breath;
others, O fair-faced one, speak of the knowledge of the internal sound (svara) as auspicious.
Indeed, the cosmic egg, its fragments, and its constituent parts were created by sound alone;
sound is the direct Great Lord (Maheśvara), the agent of both creation and dissolution.
There is no secret higher than the knowledge of sound; there is no wealth higher than the knowledge of sound.

No knowledge superior to the knowledge of one's own voice has been seen or heard. Through the strength of one's voice, one may slay an enemy; likewise, through the strength of one's voice, there is the acquisition of friends, the attainment of fortune, fame, and happiness.
The attainment of a daughter [in marriage] occurs through the strength of the voice; by the voice, one gains an audience with the king;
through the voice, there is success with the deities; and by the voice, a ruler of the earth is brought under control.
(23) By the voice, one reaches a country, and likewise, food is obtained through the strength of the voice.
One should ward off impurities through the power of the vowels, whether short or long.
O fair-faced one, there is no reality whatsoever superior to the knowledge of the vowels, including all the Śāstras, Purāṇas, Smṛtis, and Vedāṅgas.
All things beginning with name-and-form are false; there is delusion regarding all things as long as the truth has not been realized by the foolish who are bewildered by ignorance.
This treatise on the rising of breaths (Svarodaya) is the most excellent among all scriptures.
It is like the flame of a lamp for the purpose of illuminating the jar that is the self;
it should not be told to anyone else whatsoever, even for the sake of answering a question.
Therefore, this must be known by oneself, by the self within the self.
There is no need for a lunar day, nor a constellation, nor an auspicious planet, nor a deity;
nor is there need for *viṣṭi*, *vyatīpāta*, *vaidhṛti*, and the like, nor any ill-omened conjunction (*kuyoga*). Therefore, O Goddess, such [inauspicious conditions] shall never exist.
When the strength of the breath is pure and attained, every result is indeed auspicious.
(30) The channels situated within the body are multiform and very extensive;
they must always be known by the wise for the sake of understanding one's own body. (31)
Emerging from the very sprout above the bamboo-stem of the navel-center,
seventy-two thousand channels are established within the body;
therein resides the Kuṇḍalī power, coiled in the shape of a serpent.
Then there are ten channels extending upwards and ten established downwards;
two by two, the channels extending transversely number twenty-four.
However, the ten principal channels are the carriers of the ten vital winds.
The channels (nāḍīs), accompanied by wind and the body, extend horizontally and upwards;
they are all situated within the body like a wheel and are supported by the vital breath (prāṇa).
Among them, ten are preeminent, and among those ten, three are supreme.
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā as the third; Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and Yaśasvinī;
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī as the tenth.
Iḍā is situated on the left side, and Piṅgalā is said to be on the right;
Suṣumnā is in the middle region, while Gāndhārī is in the left eye.
Hastijihvā is in the right [eye], and Pūṣā is in the right ear.
Yaśasvinī is in the left ear, and Ālaṃbuṣā is in the face;
Kuhū is in the region of the genitals, while Śaṅkhinī is in the root-place (the anus).
Thus, these ten channels remain, having taken recourse to the gates.
Piṅgalā, iḍā, and suṣumnā are situated within the path of the vital breath (prāṇa).
These ten channels are established within the center of the body. I shall now state the names of these channels as well as those of the winds.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
nāga, kūrma, kṛkala, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
Prāṇa always dwells in the heart, and apāna in the region of the anus.
The *samāna* wind is located at the region of the navel, while the *udāna* resides in the middle of the throat.
The *vyāna* pervades the bodies; these are the ten principal winds.
The five beginning with *prāṇa* are well-known, as are the five winds beginning with *nāga*.
And I shall also declare the five locations of these:

the *nāga* is said to be in belching; the *kūrma* is traditionally taught to be in opening the eyes; the *kṛkala* is to be known as that which produces sneezing; and *devadatta* is in yawning. (45–46)
Even when one has died, the all-pervading Dhanañjaya does not abandon [the body];
these, in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), wander through all the channels (*nāḍīs*).
One should clearly perceive the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) from within the center of the body.
By means of the three channels—iḍā, piṅgalā, and suṣumnā—the wise one [should practice].
Iḍā is to be known as being on the left, and piṅgalā is remembered as being on the right;
the channel iḍā is situated on the left, and from there piṅgalā extends outwards.
The moon resides in the iḍā, and the sun in the piṅgalā;
Suṣumnā is in the form of Śambhu, and Śambhu is in the nature of the Haṃsa.
The letter *ha* is said to be the exhalation, while inhalation is by means of the letter *sa*.
The letter *ha* is the form of Śiva, and the letter *sa* is said to be Śakti.
The Moon, whose nature is Śakti, abides as the flow of the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*); and the Sun, whose nature is Śambhu, is the flow of the right channel (*dakṣanāḍī*).‖51–52‖
Whatever gift is given by the wise when the breath is established in the letter *Sa*,
that gift shall become multiplied ten million times ten millionfold in this world of living beings.
By this, the yogi, with a one-pointed and concentrated mind, should discern [the state].
One should indeed perceive everything on the path of the moon and the sun.
One should meditate upon the reality (tattva) when the vital breath (jīva) is steady, never when it is unsteady;
for him, there shall be the attainment of his desired goal, as well as great gain and victory. ||54-55||
Those people who always practice the union of the moon and the sun will have knowledge of the past and the future come into their hands.
On the left, she shall be in the form of nectar, the supreme nourishment for the world.
One should always produce the world from the right-moving portion.
The middle [current] is cruel and wicked in all actions;
the left [current] is the bestower of success in all auspicious undertakings.
In exiting, the left [channel] is auspicious; in entering, the right is auspicious.
The Moon should be known as even (samas), while the Sun is always uneven (viṣama). The Moon is female, the Sun is male; the Moon is fair, the Sun is dark.
One should perform gentle activities by means of the flow of the lunar channel (candranāḍī);
one should perform fierce actions by means of the flow of the solar channel (sūryanāḍī);
and by means of the flow of the Suṣumnā, one attains the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation.

In the bright fortnight the moon [rises] first, while in the other [the dark fortnight] the sun [rises first]; they say that for three days each, starting from the first day of the lunar month, both have risen earlier.
In the bright and dark fortnights, the moon and the sun should be known to rise at two and a half ghaṭikās [after sunrise].

Just as [the breath] carries sixty ghaṭīs in sequence within a single day, one should indicate that among those ghaṭīs, the five elements flow. They say that the days correspond to the [forward] progression; in the reverse [order], one should avoid them.

In the bright fortnight she is the left [channel], and in the dark fortnight she is the right; the yogin whose mind is absorbed in that should know her from the first day [of the lunar month] onward. One should restrain the moon at night, and restrain the sun by day.
Thus, that yogi who is constantly devoted to this practice has no doubt in this matter.
(66) The sun is bound by the sun, and the moon is bound by the moon;
he who understands this procedure brings the three worlds under his control in an instant. (67)
If there is rising by way of the lunar path and setting by the solar path, then those collections of qualities will be contrary; one should avoid such a state.
On the days of Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon, the left channel (vāmanāḍikā) prevails.
She bestows success in all undertakings, especially during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa).
On the days of the Sun, Mars, and Saturn, the right channel (dakṣanāḍikā) should be remembered for active tasks, especially during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa).
First the wind blows, and secondly likewise the fire;
third the earth blows, and fourth the water-element should blow.
These five arise in sequence for two and a half ghaṭikās each.
Successively, in each individual channel, there is the distinct emergence of the principles (tattvas).
Within a day and night, twelve transits (saṃkrāntis) are to be known;
[they occur] when the moon is in Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpio, Capricorn, and Pisces.
Aries, Leo, Aquarius, Libra, Gemini, and Sagittarius are to be known as rising in the south; this is the determination of the auspicious and inauspicious.
The moon should remain in the northeast, and the sun in the southwest.
When there is an expansion in the right channel (dakṣanāḍī), one should not go toward the south or west;
when there is a flow in the left practice (vāmācāra), one should not go toward the east or north. For him who has gone [there], there is fear of obstacles; he does not return. (75–76)
Therefore, the wise who desire the welfare of all should not go there;
for when one has arrived there at that time, death itself is certain, without a doubt.
When the moon transits the sun on the second day of the bright fortnight, [one should avoid it].
When [the planet] Saumya is present, it is seen to bestow gain upon men, and happiness arises.
When the Sun is at sunrise and the Moon is at moonrise, all undertakings—whether occurring by day or by night—are accomplished. (78–79)
When the moon is present at the time of the sun, or when the moon rises at sunrise, there will be agitation, quarrel, and loss; it obstructs all that is auspicious.
Wise men declare this to be the movement of the sun, for they determine even the knowledge of what is otherwise inaccessible.
But for one joined with breath during the flow of the cool-rayed [moon], the result would be otherwise.
Now, the contrary characteristic:
when at the time of dawn there occurs a contrary rising.
The Sun moves in the place of the Moon, and the Moon is in the place of the Sun.
In the first [house], there is agitation of mind; in the second, loss of wealth;
in the third, departure is declared; and in the fourth, the destruction of what is dear.
In the fifth [period], one should predict the destruction of the kingdom; in the sixth, the loss of all wealth;
in the seventh, the sufferings of disease; and in the eighth, death.
When [the wind] blows in a contrary manner during these three periods for eight days, [the same results follow].
In that case, it is said to yield an evil result, though it is slightly auspicious.
When the Moon is in the east at dawn and at midday, and the Sun is in the west at evening, then victory is always obtained; one should avoid the opposite situation.
Whether on the left or even on the right, wherever Śiva moves, one should first place that foot down; thus the journey becomes a bestower of success.
The moon (the left foot) should always be placed evenly, while the sun (the right foot) should always be placed unevenly.
Setting Pūrṇapāda at the forefront, a journey becomes a bestower of success.
On a Monday, four steps are auspicious, and on a Sunday, five steps;
traveling in this manner is excellent and shall accomplish the three worlds. (88–89)
In whichever limb the wind flows, by the friction of that limb against the hand,
one who has risen from sleep obtains the desired fruit upon touching the face. Likewise, this applies when accepting what is given by another, or even when departing from one's house.
If a vein flows in a limb, one should grasp that hand or foot;
there will be no loss, no quarrel, no thorns, nor will it be pierced.
One returns happy and indeed free from all calamities.
It bestows auspiciousness upon gurus, kinsmen, kings, ministers, and others;
indeed, when all its limbs are complete, the accomplishment of one's purpose resides in the mind.
Enemies, thieves, unrighteousness, righteousness, and the defeat of other disputants [are likewise attained].

Indeed, those who desire victory, gain, and happiness should perform [auspicious rites] during the waning moon (Riktā). However, some say that when the moon is in the Dūradeśa state, one should undertake a journey to a distant land; but when the sun is in the Dīpta state, one should go to a nearby place. || 94–95 ||
Whatever was previously indicated as gain and so forth, that entire range of equal passion arises non-conceptually within the full channels;
whereas that which was previously explained as being inverted occurs in the empty channel.
It arises exactly as spoken by the Omniscient One and not otherwise.
Indeed, in worldly affairs, in exorcism, in spells for hatred and deception, or when threatened by an angry master or thieves, those situated in the full [houses] are terrifying. ||97-98||
On a long journey, the auspicious Moon [nāḍī] grants success in one's desired goals without obstacles;
for matters concerning entry, the solar nāḍī is praised. An unsuitable [nāḍī] may be suitable for a particular time, while even a suitable place may be unsuitable.
The living soul, bound by its actions, should conduct itself just as Rudra does. When the moon moves, it endures [the heat]; the sun brings about subjection through its power.
In the Suṣumṇā there is liberation; the one God is established in three ways.
When auspicious and inauspicious activities are performed day and night, then,
in accordance with those activities, the movement of the channels (nāḍī) should be regulated.
Now, [the description of] Iḍā.
In stable works, in ornamentation, in traveling long distances, as well as in a hermitage, in a temple of Dharma, in the gathering of goods, and in the consecration of ponds,
wells, tanks, and so forth, as well as of pillars and deities; ||103||

During a journey, a gift-giving, a marriage, or the wearing of clothes, ornaments, and finery; during rites for peace (śāntika) and prosperity (pauṣṭika); during the use of divine herbs or elixirs (rasāyana);
upon seeing one's own master or a friend; and during trade or the collection of grain. || 104-105 ||
The moon is auspicious for entering a house, service, agriculture, sowing seeds, performing auspicious rites, making a treaty, and departing;
it is also favorable for undertakings such as beginning one's studies and meeting with kinsmen. 106.
In the liberation through Dharma and in Dharma itself, in initiation and in the accomplishment of mantras;

in the knowledge of time and in the Sūtra, as well as in the tradition concerning the four-footed house; in the medical treatment of diseases at the proper time, and likewise in the awakening of the Master. || 107–108 ||
In mounting elephants and horses, in the binding of archers, elephants, and horses, in assisting others, and likewise in the depositing of treasures;
in singing, instrumental music, and the like, in dancing, and in the investigation of the science of dance (nṛtya-śāstra).
And when entering a city or a village settlement; when wearing a sectarian mark (tilaka) or a parasol;

during affliction, grief, or despondency; when one is feverish or even in a state of fainting; upon meeting with kinsmen or one's master; and when gathering food, wood, and other such things. || 110–111 ||

O fair-faced one, it is declared that when the *iḍā* [channel] flows, there is success in adorning women with ornaments such as teeth [tooth-sticks], in the arrival of rain, in the worship of gurus, in the movement of those afflicted by poison,
and in practices such as the cultivation of yoga.
In this matter as well, one should avoid wind, fire, and space;
all undertakings, whether occurring by day or by night, are accomplished. For all auspicious deeds, the movement of the moon is highly recommended.
Then Piṅgalā [spoke] regarding the recitation and teaching of harsh and cruel sciences,
as well as sexual union with women, visiting prostitutes, and boarding large ships. ||115||
In cases of failed undertakings, drinking liquor, practicing heroic mantras and the like, being overwhelmed, destruction of the land and so forth, administering poison to enemies,
the study of [forbidden] scriptures, going on hunts, and the sale of animals. ||116||
In the grinding, splitting, and breaking of bricks, wood, stone, and gems;
in the practice of movement, in mechanical arts, and in climbing difficult mountains; in gambling, in theft, and in the riding and driving of elephants, horses, and chariots.
In physical exertion, in the rites of killing and summoning, in the accomplishment of the six rites and so forth,
in the subduing of yakṣiṇīs, yakṣas, vetālas, poisons, spirits, and the like,
and likewise in mounting donkeys, camels, buffaloes, elephants, and horses; ||119||
In crossing the flood of river waters, in medicine, in writing and engraving;
in killing, bewildering, paralyzing, causing enmity, uprooting, and subjugating;
in inciting, attracting, agitating, giving, and in buying and selling—120–121.
The Sun is auspicious for summoning spirits, for causing enmity, for the suppression of enemies,
for fighting foes with sword in hand, for enjoyment, for an audience with a king,
for eating, for bathing, for legal proceedings, and for fiery undertakings. (122)

In cases of weak digestion, for subjugating women and similar rites, and for all types of mobile and cruel activities, the wise should always perform the *śayana* (lying down) rite during the *sūryavāha* (sun's transit).
||123|| All cruel deeds and various types of mobile rites [should likewise be performed].
These are accomplished by means of the sun; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Now, when the vital breath flows in the *suṣumnā* for a moment, or in the left for a moment, or in the right for a moment—
And that [channel] is to be known as Suṣumnā; she is remembered as the remover of all effects.
The fire situated within that channel blazes with the form of Time (Kāla).
One should know it to be like poison, the destroyer of all effects.‖125–126‖
When the two channels of anyone flow by overstepping their proper sequence, then one should know that misfortune awaits him; there is no doubt in this.
One should predict an unfavorable state when [the breath] flows for a moment in the left and a moment in the right.
O fair-faced one, the contrary result should be known and understood;
the wise know the movement of both [planets] to be like poison.
One should not perform cruel or gentle rites, for all such actions would become fruitless.

In matters of life and death, in questions of gain and loss, victory and defeat, and in times of adversity or misfortune, one should call to mind the Lord of the World. When the Lord is meditated upon, all undertakings— such as the practice of yoga and other actions— are accomplished.

Nothing else should be performed there by those who desire the happiness of victory and gain. When the *suṣumnā* is being carried by the Sun again and again, one may bestow a curse or grant a boon; otherwise, it is entirely different.
At the time of the transition through the channels and during the union with reality (tattva),
one should not perform any auspicious act whatsoever, such as meritorious deeds or giving.
Wherever there is the arising of the Uneven (viṣama), one should not even contemplate it with the mind.
For him, travel brings ruin; there is no doubt that death and suffering will follow.
When the moon is in front, on the left, or above, and the sun is on the right, below, or behind—this distinction between full and empty must always be understood by the teachers. 134–135.
The messenger should be known as auspicious when situated on the left path, above, to the left, in front, behind, to the right, or below, having arrived via the solar course (sūryavāha).
He is without beginning, uneven, at a joint, without food, and undisturbed.
When one dissolves into the supreme subtle [reality], that is called "Sandhyā" by the wise.
They say, "This is not the Veda, this is the Veda"; yet no such Veda exists.
That by which the Supreme Self is known—that is the Veda, and it is called the Veda.
"They do not say that twilight is a junction; rather, twilight is declared to be the junction.
The breath situated at the junction is uneven; that is called the junction, and that is said to be the junction.
Thus ends the classification of the channels.
Now, regarding the determination of reality,
the venerable Goddess said:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O deliverer from the entire cycle of worldly existence!"
"O Lord, tell me the secret that resides within your heart. The Lord said:
"Indeed, apart from the secret knowledge of the vowels (svarajñāna), there is no chosen deity whatsoever."
The yogi who delights in the knowledge of the *Svaras* is considered the supreme yogi.

From the five principles (*pañcatattva*) arises creation; within each principle, a principle dissolves. The five principles are the supreme principle, yet beyond the principles is the stainless (*nirañjana*).
The names of the principles (tattvas) are to be understood by yogis through the yoga of accomplishment;
one who possesses the most excellent voice knows here the evil omens of living beings.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space as well—

He who knows that the universe consists of the five elements is truly honored. Among all the living beings of the world, no body possesses a distinct reality; from the earthly realm up to the realm of truth (satyaloka), the differentiation of the channels (nāḍīs) is unique in each case.
Five risings are proclaimed, either on the left or on the right.
O beautiful one, listen as I shall explain the eightfold knowledge of reality (*tattva*):
in the first is the enumeration of realities, and in the second, the junctions of the breaths.
In the third [chapter], the signs of the vowels; in the fourth, the locations alone;
in the fifth, their phonemes; and in the sixth, the vital breath itself.
In the seventh, those conjoined with their own tastes; and in the eighth, the characteristics of movement.

Thus, O lotus-eyed goddess, this eightfold vital breath, which is the equinox of the moving and the unmoving and is higher than the primordial sound (Svara), must always be observed with effort from the time of dawn; it is not otherwise. 149.
Yogins perform this rite for the purpose of deceiving Time (Kāla).
One should place the two thumbs on the ears, the two middle fingers on the two nostrils, another finger at the corners of the mouth, and [the remaining] fingers on the eyes.‖150–151‖
Within this, however, there arises the knowledge of the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth in succession;
by means of yellow, white, red, and dark spots, which are free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika),
one should gaze with a mirror and direct the breath into that [space].
A wise person should discern the knowledge of reality through its forms:
it is recorded as being square, crescent-shaped, triangular, and circular;
and space is to be known by means of dots. Thus, the characteristic of reality is defined by these forms.‖153–154‖
In the center is earth, below is water, and above flows fire;
the flow of air moves transversely, and space flows during the transition. Water is white, earth is yellow, and fire is red in color.
The wind is the dark-blue cloud, and space is the one possessing all colors. Fire is situated in the two shoulders, and the wind at the root of the navel.
Earth is in the region of the knees, water at the ends of the feet, and space in the head.
The earth is sweet in taste, and water is astringent;
fire is sharp, the wind is sour, and space is likewise pungent.
The wind should flow at a height of eight finger-breadths, and fire at four finger-breadths.
The earthen [circle] is twelve finger-breadths, and the watery is sixteen finger-breadths.
(159) Above, death; below, pacification; likewise, transfixion horizontally; one should know that paralyzing is in the center; and space is neutral everywhere. (160)
On Earth, one should perform stable rites; in the realm of Varuṇa (Water), mobile rites;
in Fire, cruel rites such as killing and expulsion; and in Wind, [similar fierce rites].
In Space, nothing at all should be performed; rather, one should practice the service of Yoga.
Emptiness prevails in all activities; no deliberation is required here.
Success is attained through earth and water; death occurs in fire, and destruction in air.
Everything regarding space is fruitless—this should be known by those who speak the truth of reality.
A long time must be known for gain on earth when [the breath] flows through the water-element at that moment;
there would be loss through fire and wind, and it would be fruitless through space.
When yellow, flowing slowly and moderately, as far as the jaw, there is a heavy sound.
The earthly wind is slightly warm and accomplishes stable tasks.
(165) That wind which flows downward, has a heavy sound, moves swiftly, is cool, remains steady, and measures sixteen finger-breadths, is the watery wind; it performs auspicious deeds. (166)
That which whirls, is extremely hot, has the luster of blood, measures four fingers [in breadth], and flows upwards— that which performs cruel deeds is the fiery (taijasa) vein.
That which is hot and cold, black in color, moves obliquely, and measures eight fingers [in breadth]— 167.
Vāyu, known as Pavana, is the accomplisher of the function of movement. That which is the wind (samīra), equal in essence (samarasa), and the bringer of the qualities of all the principles (tattva)—
one should know that to be Āmbara, which bestows yoga upon yogins.
Yellow in color, quadrangular, sweet, and situated in the center;
this earthly element (*pārthiva-tattva*) bestows enjoyment (*bhoga*), and its flow measures twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
White, resembling a half-moon, with a sweet and moist appearance.
The Varuṇa principle, which brings gain, is sixteen finger-breadths in the flow;
it is red, triangular, sharp, and flows in the upper part.
The Taijasa principle, which is radiant, is four finger-breadths in the flow.
Blue in color, circular in shape, sweet and sour in taste, and situated obliquely;
the principle of wind (māruta-tattva) is known to be eight finger-breadths in its flow,
flickering and moving everywhere, with its color, form, taste, and movement being unmanifest.
The ethereal element (*nābhasa-tattva*) bestows liberation, yet it is fruitless in all worldly undertakings. The elements of earth and water are auspicious; fire brings about mixed results;
while space and wind are inauspicious for men, causing loss and death.
Earth is in the eastern and western [directions], and fire likewise in the south;
wind is to be known in the northern direction, and space is situated in the center and the corners. Earth and water are associated with the moon, while fire belongs to the sun.
Then success is certain, without doubt, in both gentle and fierce undertakings.
During the day, the earth element brings profit; at night, water brings profit.
Fire causes death or loss; wind [brings] destruction; and the ether element may sometimes cause burning.
Regarding life, victory, gain, agriculture, financial undertakings, the purpose of mantras, inquiries concerning war, as well as going and coming—
if [the query] occurs when the Varuṇa-tattva is present, there is an enemy; on Earth (Kṣiti), it is auspicious.
If it moves elsewhere than from the air, there is loss or death; in the case of fire, it is the sky;

on earth, there is concern for the roots; for the living being, it concerns water and air; through fire, there is concern for the bodily constituents; and one should declare the void to be from the sky. ||180-181||
On earth there are those with many feet; from water and air come those with two feet; from fire alone come those with four feet; and by means of space, they are devoid of feet.
Mars is fire, the Sun is earth, and Saturn is proclaimed to be water.
Rāhu is situated in the station of air and flows through the right aperture.
Water is the Moon, Mercury is earth, Jupiter is wind, Venus is fire;
all these reside in the left channel and are determined for all undertakings.
Earth is Mercury, water is the Moon, fire is Venus,
the Sun is Mars, wind is Rāhu, Saturn is space, and Jupiter alone is thus proclaimed [to be ether].
In a query concerning travel abroad, if Rāhu has gone to the wind while the Sun is present...
Then he should be known as having set out, seeking another place.
When the Varuṇa element arrives, there is auspiciousness right there on the earth;
in the Vāyu [element], he is away from home elsewhere; and in the Agni [element], death itself shall occur.
In the earth [element], the knowledge of roots is auspicious; likewise, it is so in water.
In the fire [element], the knowledge of minerals [is auspicious]; in space, one should designate emptiness.
Contentment, nourishment, pleasure, play, victory, and joy [are the results] in earth and water.
When fire and wind are present, there is a fever and trembling for one who has traveled abroad;
when in the element of space, it is proclaimed that life has departed and death has occurred.
These twelve signs must always be diligently understood by the teachers.
One should designate the elements, beginning with earth, as being most powerful in the east, west, south, and north respectively:
earth, water, fire, air, and space.
O fair-faced one, the body should be understood as consisting of the five elements:
bone, flesh, skin, sinew, and hair as the fifth.
Earth is said to possess these five qualities; this was spoken by the knowledge of Brahman.
Semen, blood, marrow, urine, and saliva as the fifth—
these are declared to be the five qualities of water, as spoken by one possessing the knowledge of Brahman.
Hunger, thirst, sleep, lust, and likewise laziness—
The five qualities of fire (tejas) have been declared and spoken by Brahmajñāna:
running, moving, odor, contraction, and expansion.
The five qualities of air (vāyu) have been declared and spoken by Brahmajñāna.
Attachment and aversion, as well as shame, fear, and delusion as the fifth—
these are said to be the five qualities of space, as declared by the knowledge of Brahman.
Fifty palas belong to earth, and likewise forty to water.
In fire, [the attainment] occurs thirty times; in wind, twenty; and in space, ten.
On earth, attainment comes after a long time; in water, it may happen in an instant. In wind, it arises only slightly, and even when perfected in fire, it perishes.
Earth has five qualities, water four, fire two, wind two, and space one; this is the knowledge of the principles (tattva).
When the earth is blown upon, it cracks, splits, and falls apart.
In all undertakings, it yields a result corresponding to one's condition.
Dhaniṣṭhā, Rohiṇī, Jyeṣṭhā, Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, as well as Abhijit and Uttarāṣāḍhā—these are declared to be the Earth element (pṛthvītattva). ||201–202||
Pūrvāṣāḍhā, as well as Āśleṣā, Mūla, Ārdrā, and Revatī;
Uttarā Bhādrapadā and Śatabhiṣaj, O Dear One, constitute the water-element (toyatattva). Furthermore, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Puṣya, Maghā, and Pūrvā Phālgunī.

Pūrvābhādrapadā and Svātī are the fire element (tejastattva), O Dear One. Viśākhā, Uttaraphalgunī, Hasta, Citrā, Punarvasu, Āśvinī, and Mṛgaśīrṣa are declared to be the wind element (vāyutattva). || 204–205 ||
Whatever auspicious or inauspicious matter the messenger asks while situated in the *vahana-nāḍī*, all that attains success; in the *śūnya* [nāḍī], it is empty—of this there is no doubt.
Even when full, [the breath] is not a giver of success during exhalation, even if it is in the true principle (*sutattva*).
Whether it be the Sun or the Moon, [the chosen deity] bestows all accomplishments upon men when held in the grasp [of the mind].
Rāma attained victory through the *tattva*, and Dhanañjaya likewise;
yet all the Kauravas were slain in battle due to a perversion of the *tattva*. (207–208)

In some pure-souled individuals, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) for reality arises either from the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) of previous births or through the grace of the Guru. Now follows the meditation on the five principles (*pañcatattva*).
One should meditate on the seed-syllable *laṃ* as the earth, square in shape and of a beautiful yellow luster;

one who meditates on it as fragrant and with the brilliance of gold shall attain lightness of body. One should meditate on the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, belonging to Varuṇa, which is the [elemental] principle (*tattva*) and has the radiance of the half-moon.
Endurance of hunger, thirst, and the like, and immersion in water;
one should meditate on the seed-syllable *raṃ*, which is fire, triangular and red in luster;
[the results are] the consumption of abundant food and drink, and endurance of heat and fire.

One should meditate on the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, which is the wind, circular and dark-blue in luster; [through this] one attains the power of traveling through space and likewise the ability to move like a bird. One should meditate on the seed-syllable *haṃ*, which is the sky, formless and of great radiance.
Knowledge has the three periods of time as its object, and sovereignty consists of the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
Where there is no wealth, a man who possesses knowledge of the *svara* goes beyond that;
indeed, by means of the knowledge of the *svara*, the fruit is attained without effort.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, how does the great knowledge of the *Svarodaya*, which pertains to the three times, come to be, O Śaṅkara? (216)
Īśvara said:
"The inquiry into wealth, time, and victory, as well as the auspicious and inauspicious—this threefold knowledge of the three times is nothing other than this, O beautiful one. (217)
In the *tattva* is the auspicious and inauspicious action; in the *tattva* are victory and defeat;
in the *tattva* are abundance and famine; thus the *tattva* is said to consist of three parts.
(218) The Goddess said:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, in this entire ocean of worldly existence,
what is the supreme friend for men that accomplishes all their purposes?
Īśvara said:
"Prāṇa alone is the supreme friend; Prāṇa alone is the supreme companion;
there is no other kinsman equal to Prāṇa—there is none, none, O fair-faced one.
Śrī Devī said:
"How does the wind abide as the vital breath (prāṇa), and what is the nature of the body as the form of the vital breath?
How is the vital breath, moving through the principles (tattvas), known by yogins?
Śrī Śiva said:
The vital wind (māruta), residing in the midst of the city of the body, acts as its guardian.
It is said to measure ten finger-breadths (aṅgulas) upon entry and twelve finger-breadths upon exit;
it measures twenty-four finger-breadths during movement and thirty-two finger-breadths while running.
In sexual intercourse it is sixty-five [finger-breadths], and in lying down it is one hundred finger-breadths.
O Goddess, the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) is by its very nature twelve finger-breadths;
in eating and in vomiting, its movement is eighteen finger-breadths.
When the breath is diminished by one finger-breadth, it is considered the state of desirelessness (niṣkāmatā);
bliss (ānanda) occurs at the second, and the power of the poet (kavi-śakti) at the third.
At the fourth, there is perfection in speech (vācā-siddhi), and far-sighted vision (dūra-dṛṣṭi) at the fifth.
In the sixth [birth], however, there is travel through the sky; in the seventh, fierce speed;
in the eighth, the supernatural powers (siddhis); in the ninth, the nine treasures (nidhis);
in the tenth, the ten forms (daśamūrti); and in the eleventh, there shall be a shadow.
In the twelfth [state], one should drink the nectar-essence of the Gaṅgā through the movement of the *haṃsa*;
when the vital breath is full, for whom would there be anything to eat or to consume, even down to the tips of the nails?
Thus has the rule of the vital breath been proclaimed, which bestows the fruits of all undertakings.
Knowledge is known through the word of the Guru, not by means of millions of scriptures.
(229) If, by chance, the moon is not found in the east at dawn or the sun in the west at evening, it nevertheless proceeds from midday and from midnight onwards. (230)
Candra is victorious in distant warfare, while Divākara is victorious when it is near.
A quarter (pāda) that has arrived in the ascending channel (nāḍī) bestows all accomplishments.
[This applies] at the commencement of a journey, at a marriage, and upon entering a city or similar places.
Auspicious deeds always succeed during the movements of the moon,
provided that, by the conjunction of destiny, they occasionally flow for men when conjoined with their own *tattva* according to the solstice, lunar day, and lord of the day.‖232‖
He conquers the enemy army with a voice that is merely a mere throb;
yet he does not prevail over even Keshava in this world.
"Protect the life! Protect the life!"—having thus wrapped it around the limb of the living being.
The living one who chants conquers the earth alive in battle.
In rites for pacification, movement should be performed on the earth and in water;
however, it should not be performed in fire, wind, the blazing sky, nor in both together.

One should fasten the weapon with the vital breath (*jīva*), and with the vital breath alone one should draw it forth; with the vital breath one should discharge the weapon—in battle, one thus always triumphs. Having drawn in the breath of life (*prāṇapavana*), one should mount the vehicle.
One should bestow a step upon the one who has crossed over; thus one shall accomplish all tasks.
Whether the enemy's assembly is incomplete or complete, or likewise one's own force, he who abides in the perfection of reality conquers the earth alone.

Whichever channel flows in a limb, the presiding deity of that very [channel] faces those directions and bestows the fruits of all undertakings. First, the mudrā should be performed, and afterwards one should engage in battle.
For one by whom the serpent-mudrā is performed, success is attained without a doubt.
||240|| Furthermore, whether in the flow of the moon or the flow of the sun, warriors arrive desiring to fight;
the wind is well-known to the knowers of reality, and that which is emptiness is the destroyer of what is to be countered. ||241||
In whichever direction the wind blows, one should cause the battle to take place in that direction;
one will surely be victorious, there is no doubt, even if Śakra himself stands before one.
Wherever the wind flows through a channel (nāḍī), one should likewise direct the vital breath (prāṇa) toward that very limb.
Drawing [the bow] back as far as the ear, one surely conquers even Indra;
he who protects his body completely from the blows of adversaries cannot be struck by enemies, even those who are most powerful. (243–244)

When a sound is produced on the joint of the thumb and forefinger, as well as on the big toe, it should be employed at the time of battle; one who employs it will become a conqueror of even a hundred thousand targets.
When the moon moves through the sound-path, its wind resides in the center.

Standing still, one should protect the quarters of the world if desiring victory; but when one has departed, [the result] is always [otherwise]. When the messenger speaks the desired [message] at the time of the inhalation of the breath, O beautiful one, his prayer attains success; but not at all during the exhalation.
Even matters such as gains and other undertakings, when inquired about or mentioned, succeed when Jupiter enters [the ascendant];
there would be loss upon its departure.
For a man, Jupiter in the tenth house is skillful and his own; for a woman, it is praised when situated in the seventh house.
Kumbhaka occurs at the time of battle; there are three channels and a threefold path.
(249) Without the distinction between the letter *ha* and the letter *sa*, how can there be a vowel?
By means of the very word *haṃsa*, that *jīva*—which is "I"—is ever victorious. (250)
Having filled the empty house, one should conceal the victory within the living house;
for if one strikes the living house, one meets with death, whereas the empty house always protects.
Whether the questioner asks on the left or on the right, [the result follows].
In the *pūrṇa* [breath], no injury occurs; one should indicate injury in the *śūnya* [breath].
By the element of earth, there is injury in the region of the belly; by water, it occurs in the region of the feet;
by the element of fire, in the region of the thighs; and by air, in the region of the hands.‖252–253‖
The determination of the blow should be known in the head and in the element of space (*vyomatattva*).
Thus, the fivefold blow is revealed in the science of sounds (*svaraśāstra*).
At the time of battle, when the Moon is stationary, victory is certain. (Corrected: *yuddhakāle*)
When the flow of the Sun prevails as it moves forward, then victory is attained. In a situation where victory is doubtful, one should observe the middle of the channel;
when the vital breath (prāṇa) has entered the Suṣumnā, there is danger from the enemy in battle.
One should take refuge in the direction of whichever channel (nāḍī) the breath flows during battle;
then one attains victory—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
If, however, at the time of combat, the left channel (vāmanāḍī) should always flow... [corr. °kāla]
One should know that victory belongs to the defender, even if the rise of the planets favors the enemy.
However, if at the time of battle the sun should blow in a contrary direction, then one should know that the attacker will be victorious over gods, asuras, and humans. (258–259)
In battle, the enemy carries him off; therefore, a man should enter into the *vāmā* [left] path.
By moving through the equinox (*viṣuvat*), he gains his position; victory comes through the running sun.
When two questions regarding battle are posed, victory belongs to the first if it is full.

When the second [side] is indeed empty, one becomes victorious; it is not otherwise. When the full channel is at the back and the empty limb is then in front, an enemy placed in the empty position dies; there is no doubt about this.
Victory shall belong to that person whose name has an equal number of syllables when moving on the left;
the questioner on the right side, with an odd number of syllables, is the victor.
When one asks concerning the Moon, then one should predict a reconciliation.
When [the moon] is in conjunction with the Sun, then one should know the planetary conflict:
against an earthly [planet] there is an equal battle; success occurs against a watery [planet];
in battle, there is defeat against a fiery [planet], or death against a windy or even a celestial [planet].‖264–265‖
When the wind is not perceived due to signs or negligence at the time of questioning, then the wise man should diligently perform this:
having established an immovable concentration (*dhāraṇā*), he should let go of a flower from his hand.

If flowers fall upon one whose limbs are complete, or if they are absent, that is the supreme sign. Whether standing or sitting, drawing in his own vital breath and without allowing the mind to falter, he lives successfully in all undertakings.
Neither time, nor various terrible things, nor weapons, nor serpents,
nor enemies, diseases, thieves, and the like, are capable of devouring one who dwells in an empty place.
One should stabilize the vital breath (vāyu) with the life-force (jīva), and again, one should set it in motion by means of the life-force.
He plays with his own life-force constantly and wins at the game of dice in every way.
By the power of the knowledge of vowels, that which was previously fruitful becomes fruitless ten millionfold;
in this world and in the next, the knower of vowels is always powerful.
In some places, the strength of a ruler of a country may be ten thousand, a hundred thousand, or a million;
the strength of the gods, headed by Śatakratu and Surendra, would be ten million times that.
Śrī Devī said:
"You have declared that victory belongs to humans in mutual combat;
but when a battle between twins arises among men, how can there be victory? 273.
The Lord said:
One should meditate on the deity while remaining steady, and one should offer oblations into the union of the individual soul (jīva).
For such a person, there shall be the attainment of desired goals, as well as great gain and victory.
The entire world, possessing form and parts, has arisen from that which is formless.
At that very moment, that cognition becomes both with form and without form.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"O Maheśvara, you have spoken of human combat and the combat of Yama."
"Now, tell me the method for subjugating the gods of gods.
Īśvara said:
"Having drawn the moon with the sun, one should place it within the circle of the vital breath (jīva)."
It has been declared by those whose wealth is austerity that women remain under the power [of passion] from birth.
Life is seized by life; life is given to life.
Having entered the place of life, the youth becomes the bringer of life’s end.
When the women have fallen asleep at the hour of the final watch of the night, that man who drinks the life-force of Brahmā becomes a taker of the breath of children.
Having recited the eight-syllable mantra when that time has passed—[corrected: *tasmin kāle gate sati*]— [he attains his goal].
At that very moment, the moon is bestowed [upon her], and the passionate woman falls into a state of enchantment.
Whether on the bed, during dalliance, or even in the embrace of a young woman,
he who drinks the moon with the sun shall become the one whose banner is the sea-monster (Makaradhvaja).
If Śiva is embraced by Śakti during the *prasaṅga* (conjunction) in either the right or left [channel],
he who bestows that [union] at that very moment may delude even a hundred passionate women.
The union occurs nine, seven, three, or five times during the solar asterism (*sūryabha*).
Having performed [the recitation] twice, four times, and six times, the passionate woman becomes submissive.
Having drawn in the sun and moon and pressed them with the serpent upon the lower lip,
one should touch the great lotus with bliss and perform this again and again.
As long as she has not reached the state of sleep, the lotus remains with its breath;
afterwards, at the proper time, it awakens and its throat and eyes are sucked.
By this method, a lover may bring all women under his control.
"This must not be spoken of to another; she is the eternally commanding Supreme Goddess. Thus ends the section on subjugation. Now begins the section on the womb (garbha).
When a woman who has reached her fertile period arrives on the fifth day,
the birth of a son occurs through union during the conjunction of the sun and the moon. When the earth and water flow together, one should take *śaṅkhavallī* with cow's milk.
One should speak these words on behalf of the husband alone; grant pride with these three words:
"A woman who has bathed after her menses should drink [the mixture], and she should employ the seasonal gift (ṛtudāna);
thus she gives birth to a lion among men, endowed with beauty and charm. (288–289)

One should join the gift of the season with the Suṣumnā as the carrier of the sun. A man who is born here with a deformed body or lacking limbs [is affected] when the day and night have odd-numbered digits, and when the lord of the day has odd-numbered digits.
Through the principles (tattvas) of the moon, the eye, and fire, a barren woman may obtain a son.
At the onset of the season, the sun belongs to men and the moon to women;
when the union of both occurs, a barren woman may obtain a son.
At the commencement of the season, the Sun [is the operative force] for men, and at the end of the semen, the Moon [is so] for women;
by this sequential application, he does not take up the wood of destiny.
When the lunar channel is active at the time of inquiry, then a daughter shall be born in the womb.
Then Sūrya becomes the son; the embryo of two [elements] is destroyed.
On earth there is a daughter, in water a son, but in wind a girl;
in fire there would be a miscarriage of the embryo, and in ether a neuter child.‖294–295‖
If the messenger arrives under the Moon, it is female; under the Sun, male; and on the intermediate path, neuter.
In a query regarding pregnancy, when the messenger arrives at the full [digit], a son is born;
at the void, a void [child]; at the junction (yuga), twins; and at the transition (saṃkrama), there is a miscarriage.
O beautiful one, the knower of reality should understand that which has been described:

conception occurs when the breath is in the east (mārute), resulting in suffering; when it is known to be in the north (dikṣu), the child is famous; and when in the west (vāruṇe), he is endowed with happiness. ||297||
In the fire [element], there is miscarriage or a short life;
one born in earth is fortunate and endowed with wealth.
He is wealthy, possessed of happiness, and enjoys pleasures, established in prosperity.
In the principle of Varuṇa, the fetus may perish while still in the womb;
in that of Mahendra, there is the birth of a fine son; in that of Varuṇa, a daughter shall be born;
and in the remaining [principles], there will be loss of the fetus or death immediately after birth. || 299–300 ||
"The moon is situated within the sun, and the sun is situated within the moon;
this must be known quickly from the Guru, not through the Vedas nor by tens of millions of scriptures.
Thus ends the section on the Womb (Garbha-prakaraṇa).
Now, regarding the fruit of the year:
on the morning of the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the discerning yogi should observe the differentiation of the principles during the southern and northern solstices. (302)
When the moon rises, if [the wind] blows here in its true nature, there will be prosperity arising from all crops, as well as earth, water, and air. However,
if it blows through the principles of fire and space, there will be terrible fear and famine according to the reality of the time.
Thus should the fruit of the true state (tattva) be known for the year, the month, and even the day.
When it is middling, it becomes cruel and wicked in all undertakings;
it bestows suffering such as the ruin of the country, great diseases, afflictions, and hardships.

At the moment of the sun's transition into Aries (meṣa-saṃkrānti), one who contemplates the truth should examine the changes in the voice; he should then declare the results for the year for the people,
according to the principles of earth and the other elements, which produce results for the day, month, and year.
And just as a beautiful thing may be marred by space, wind, and fire, [so too may prosperity be ruined];
yet, if the earth element prevails, there shall be abundance of food, growth of the kingdom, the earth shall abound with crops, there will be much rain, and likewise happiness. (307–308)
If the water element prevails, there will be excessive rain, abundance of food, health, and happiness;
likewise, the earth will be rich in crops. However, if [the fire element prevails], there will be famine, the ruin of the kingdom, and the destruction of all that has been produced.
If the fire element flows when the rain is already slight, there will be even less rain;
there will be fear due to portents and calamities, and the seasonal plagues (īti) will be minor.
If the air element flows at the time of the Aries transit, [the following occurs]: ||310-311||
If the element of space (vyomatattva) flows at the time of the Aries transit (meṣasaṃkrānti),
even then emptiness (śūnyatā) is to be known for crops and happiness. When the breath enters in full, the crop is accomplished through that very element.
When the sun and moon have changed their positions, the conjunction bestows all accomplishments (siddhis).
When it is uneven, the fire-element (vahnitattva) shall arise, and only the sky is perceived;
one should perform that [ritual], for the collection of goods will result in high prices within two months.
When the sun enters [the solar node], the channel moves toward the moon at the end;
through the union of ether, wind, and fire, the surface of the earth becomes Raurava.
Thus ends the section on the year.
Now, the section on diseases: One's own disease occurs in the earth element; in water, it is caused by the mother of water;
in fire, it is caused by a *śākinī* residing in the courtyard of a planet; and [in air], it is due to the fault of the ancestors. (316)
If the messenger first enters the void and subsequently enters the full, then even one who is unconscious will certainly live; this is because he asks for the sake of that [life].
In whichever limb the life-force resides, he asks while remaining situated in that very place.
Then that living being survives, even if afflicted by diseases.
When the messenger wind blows from the south and speaks with fierce syllables, then that living being survives; in the case of the moon, the result will be neutral.
If one assumes the form of a living being and observes that form,
then for a question concerning life, the result will be life itself, provided the breath is situated within the living being.
Likewise, when the breath enters the left channel, or the right, or whichever vehicle [of the breath] it occupies.
If the messenger stands there and asks, his success is certain; of this there is no doubt. (321) In the inquiry, if the vital breath (jīva) is situated below, the person certainly lives;
if the vital breath is situated moving upwards, the living one goes to the abode of Yama. (322)

If the questioner asks when the lunar day (tithi) is Riktā during a query involving reversed syllables, the opposite result should be understood when there is an odd planetary rising (viṣamodaya). If Jupiter is situated in the place of the Moon while the questioner is in the place of the Sun, [the result is contrary].

Then, even if surrounded by hundreds of physicians, he is deprived of life. When the vital breath (jīva) is situated in Piṅgalā and the messenger asks on the left, then too the sick person dies, unless Maheśvara himself is his protector. ||324-325||
In this world, when one of the elements undergoes a transformation, men become overcome by disease;
when both of these occur, there is the loss of kinsmen and friends on both sides.
Death shall occur through a reversal [of the elements].
(326) Thus ends the section on diseases. Now begins the section on time.
At the beginning of the month, the fortnight, and the year, in due order,
the wise man should examine the time of dissolution according to the movement of the breath.
The lamp consisting of the five elements is moistened with the oil of Śiva.
One should protect [the breath] with the solar wind (sūryavāta), and the living being (prāṇī) will become stable.
If, having bound the wind (māruta), one binds the sun,
then through practice the living being lives even when the time of the sun has been cheated.
The moon flows from the sky and sprinkles the lotuses of the body;
through constant practice of the yoga of action, one becomes immortal by taking refuge in the moon. One should restrain the moon at night, and the sun should be restrained during the day.

Thus, that yogi who is constantly devoted to this practice has no doubt in this matter. When the vital wind flows through only one [channel] for a day and night, then death shall occur for him within three full years.
For one whose breath always moves through the Piṅgalā for two days and nights,
his lifespan is declared by the knowers of reality to be two years.
For one in whom the wind flows for three nights while remaining in a single channel—
Then the wise declare that his lifespan is one year. If the moon should flow continuously at night and the sun by day,
one should know that his death will indeed occur within six months.
When the sun is seen reflected in water by means of its reflection,
it is diminished in the south, west, north, and east respectively by six, three, two, and one months;
in the center there would be a hole for ten days, and on that day it is filled with smoke.

The lifespan has been clearly declared even by the omniscient, best of sages. A messenger wearing red, saffron, or black garments, with teeth broken, shaven-headed, his body smeared with oil, holding a rope in his hand, dejected, and with eyes full of tears— ||336||
Bhasma, Aṅgāraka, Kapāla, Pāśa, Musalī, and Sūryā come toward him who stands in the state of Kālī-Śūnya, accompanied by Gadā and honored by Kālānala.
Suddenly there is a transformation of the mind; suddenly there is Puruṣottama.
The sudden malfunctioning of the sense organs is a sign of impending death.
When the body becomes cold and its natural state undergoes a transformation, that is *ariṣṭa* (the omen of death) in brief; now learn it from me in detail.

He who delights in wicked words and even in impure words, yet later performs penance—for him there is death; of this there is no doubt. He for whom the sound "huṃ" is cool and the hissing sound is like fire—

For one who [sees] the Great Physician, death shall certainly occur. Having gazed for a moment at the tongue, Viṣṇupada, Dhruva, Surapada, the auspicious Mātṛkā-maṇḍala, Arundhatī, Amṛtagu, Śukra, or Dhruva; ||| 341 ||
If a man sent ahead does not clearly perceive even one of these before him,
he will certainly enter the mouth of Death here after a year has passed.
[He sees] the sun's orb without rays, and the fire of the moon-crested one [Śiva].
Having seen that his life will last for only eleven months, a man does not live beyond that. If one sees feces, urine, gold, or silver in a pond—
either directly or in a dream— he will not live for ten months.
If one sees at some point an island of gold mixed with iron,
or deformed beings, he will not live for nine months.
One whose limbs are stout suddenly becomes emaciated, and one who is emaciated suddenly attains stoutness.

Even if one who was cruel becomes golden-hued, or one with a dark complexion becomes brave, or a coward becomes wise, or a man skilled in unrighteousness becomes peaceful, or a restless man becomes tranquil—their very nature undergoes such change; yet, such a person lives for only eight months. (346)
There will be pain in the palm of the hand and likewise at the root of the tongue, and the blood shall be black;
yet where it is pierced, one does not grow weary as long as it is seen with the eye.
A man lives for seven months indeed;
he whose three middle fingers are not curved and whose throat withers without illness [shall live for seven months].
Due to dullness, by virtue of being asked questions again and again, he goes to destruction within six months. For him,
there is no memory whatsoever regarding the skin of the breasts.
He will certainly, in the fifth month, become mounted upon the aggregates (skandhas).
For one whose inner light does not flash and whose two eyes are afflicted,
death is declared to be certain in the fourth month.
If one's teeth and testicles are not afflicted by even the slightest pain,
that man will certainly become subject to the power of Time after three months.
Or, by whatever means Time, though situated at a distance, may be perceived— [351] — [one should act accordingly].
I shall state that in brief, as it has been taught in the Śiva-āgama:
having gone to a solitary, secluded place and placing the sun behind one's back,
one should, with a concentrated mind, observe one's own shadow at the region of the throat.
Then one should gaze into the sky [reciting] "Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Brahman.
Having recited this one hundred and eight times, one then beholds Śaṅkara—
Hara, who resembles pure crystal and assumes manifold forms.
Through the practice of yoga for six months, one becomes the lord of those who move upon the earth;
after two years, O Lord, he himself becomes the master, the creator and the destroyer. By that means, he then attains knowledge of the three times as well as supreme bliss.
Through the yoga of constant practice, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain.
That yogi who beholds that form, black in color, in the stainless sky for six months, meets his death; of this there is no doubt. (356–357)
If it is yellow, one should predict disease; if red, fear; if blue, loss. However, if it is of various colors, great success is proclaimed.
Furthermore, destruction occurs respectively in the foot, the ankle, and the abdomen.
When one's own arms wither away, one will certainly die;
there is no doubt that if the left arm withers, one's wife will perish. If it is the right arm, there is indeed the loss of kinsmen; death should be predicted within a month.
Death without the head occurs in a month; without the calves, in eight days;
through the loss of the anus, in eight [days]; and by the disappearance of the shadow, at that very moment.
When the sun has moved behind the back in the morning, the shadow [disappears] in an instant, as do the fingers and the lower lip.
If a man sees his own shadow as half its usual size, he dies immediately thereafter.
If he sees it without its ears, hands, mouth, sides, or heart, he dies within half a moment.
Indeed, if a man is confused about the directions and perceives only his head, he lives for six months.
If the Sun should flow continuously for one to sixteen days for anyone,
his death will indeed occur within the remaining portion of the month. When the Sun flows in its entirety and the Moon is not seen at all, [death follows].

Death occurs within a fortnight, as declared by the Knower of Time (Kālajña). When urine, feces, and wind move simultaneously, then he should be known as having departed; he will certainly die within ten days.
The moon appears full and the sun is no longer seen; death will occur within a month—thus it was declared by the Knower of Time. Arundhatī, Dhruva, and the three steps of Viṣṇu [are likewise signs].
Those whose life-span is exhausted do not behold the fourth circle of the Mothers (mātṛmaṇḍala).
Arundhatī is the tongue, and Dhruva is the tip of the nose;
the eyebrows are to be known as Viṣṇupada, and the Tāraka is the circle of the Mothers.
If one has nine eyebrows, seven sounds, five stars, and three nostrils,
it is declared that such a person will certainly die within a single day.
One should gaze while pressing the corners of the eyes slightly with the fingers.
When the drop (*bindu*) is no longer seen, one will die within ten days. By visiting sacred sites, giving gifts, performing austerities, and doing meritorious deeds,
as well as through recitations, meditation, and yoga, the deception of Time (*kālavañcanā*) is achieved.
These humors (doṣas) as well as the bodily constituents and wastes destroy the body;
however, the wind (vāyu) should be known as balanced when it increases strength and vitality.
Therefore, the body must be protected, since it is the means for accomplishing dharma and other goals.
Through the practice of yoga, even those who are difficult to master become attainable;
however, those who are impossible to master destroy one's life, and there is no remedy for that.
[This applies to] those in whose heart the non-dual [reality] constantly vibrates.
This secret power is capable of destroying the mass of darkness;
for those men who possess the beautiful luster of the unbroken moon, there is no fear of death even in their dreams.
The *iḍā* should be known as the Gaṅgā, and the *piṅgalā* as the river Yamunā;
one should know that the *sarasvatī* is in the middle, and Prayāga and the others are likewise situated there.
First, the practice has been described, which produces immediate conviction.
The yogi, having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), should perform the uḍḍiyānabandha.
Inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka) as the third—
these must always be known by yogis for the sake of purifying the body.
Pūraka brings about growth as well as the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātus).
Kumbhaka effects stabilization and increases the protection of the vital life-force (jīva). Recaka removes sin; one should practice it so that one may attain the state of Yoga.
Thereafter, one should remain as if in combat and effect the binding of the dissolution (layabandha). One should restrain the innate wind (sahajavāyu) according to one's capacity;
the wise practitioner should exhale through the lunar path and fill [the lungs] through the solar path.
The sun drinks the moon, and the moon drinks the sun;
through their mutual temporal relationship, one may live as long as the moon and stars exist.
The channel flows within one's own body; therefore, block that channel.
Without releasing the seal of the mouth, one becomes a youth; indeed, one generates the vital breath (pavana).
One should block the ends of the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears with the fingers.
This should be known as "The Arising of Reality" (tattvodaya), the beloved "Six-Faced Practice" (ṣaṇmukhīkaraṇa). || 382-383 ||
Its form, its movement, its taste, and this characteristic of its mandala—
the man who knows these in this world becomes a knower of the path even through mere association.
Free from desire and partless, the yogi should not think of anything at all.
Having rendered the latent impression (*vāsanā*) transcendent (*unmanā*), one conquers time with ease.
The power that is the altar of the universe is perceived by the two eyes;
for him whose mind remains fixed there for even a single watch (*yāma*) in this world, [liberation is attained].‖385–386‖
His lifespan increases constantly by the measure of three *ghaṭikās*.
This was stated of old by Śiva in the *Siddhaguṇagahvara-tantra*:
"Those who, having assumed the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), properly restrain the vital breath (*pavana*) located in the anus and [draw it] upward..."
Having restrained that vital breath (*prāṇa*), conquered through the stages, within her lower aperture by means of the power of *prāṇa*,
and having brought it— now become one— with the opening of the *suṣumnā* and led it into the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*),
those certain fortunate ones, devoted to the feet of Śiva, depart upon the path of space. (388)
The yogi who knows this and recites it constantly becomes liberated from all suffering and attains his desired fruit.
Wherever a man possesses knowledge of the vowels, there Fortune shall reside at the soles of his feet.
And throughout his entire body, he shall always experience happiness.
Just as the *praṇava* is among all the Vedas and the sun is among the Brahmins,
so too is a man who knows the true nature of the self worthy of worship in the world of mortals.
One may know the three channels and likewise the knowledge of reality;
yet even a million or ten million elixirs cannot equal that [knowledge].
[It is superior to] the giver of a single syllable who discerns the distinctions of the channels.
On this earth, there is no object that, having given it away, one would become free from debt.
O Goddess, the reality of one's own voice, as well as battle, subjugation,
women, conception, and disease— these are said to be determined by half a digit (kalā).
Thus set forth in the world, it is renowned among accomplished yogis;
recited during lunar or solar eclipses, it bestows success upon those who read it.
Seated in the place of the vital breaths (svarasthāna), one should take little sleep and little food.
"He who knows [this] should meditate upon the Supreme Self; he shall become [that Supreme Self].
Thus ends the Svarodaya Śāstra in the dialogue between the illustrious Śiva and Pārvatī.
